attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, not a quotation.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps 'does not seem to be enough', which matches the source. It is an impressionistic, hedged observation, not a categorical statement that the public internet is exhausted.

contract.note: The contract marks plain_reading true, but 'doesn't seem to be enough' is hedged. Policy limits plain readings to firm language. The contract also has to supply its own meaning for 'enough', so the speaker's words never fixed a testable threshold.

evidence.note: Dated preprint from June 2023. It forecasts that internet text 'may soon' become a limit. It does not measure insufficiency on the post date.
AP press release (company disclosure) on OpenAI licensing AP's archive. Licensing does not isolate data scarcity from quality, rights or commercial reasons.
Preprint from 2022 projecting that high-quality text would run out, likely before 2026, and lower-quality text much later. This is a forecast, not evidence of the state on the post date.

reviews.rationale: The statement is hedged ('doesn't seem') and gives no measure of what counts as enough, so policy does not score it. The evidence would not settle it either way: e1 and e3 forecast future scarcity, and e2 shows licensing without showing that public data fell short.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The revision restores 'much of what it needed' and 'without going through all your personal data'. In context, the claim is about an alternative to the prevailing data-greedy general paradigm.

contract.note: The contract counts any learning approach with 'useful real-world capabilities' as an alternative. Read that way, narrow systems such as robot locomotion would falsify the claim trivially. That stretches the claim against Marcus, who meant a paradigm that learns broadly enough to be effective in the world, as a replacement for the current data-greedy approach.

evidence.note: Correctly dated DayDreamer preprint from 2022 showing narrow robot skills learned from interaction. That does not show a general paradigm effective in the world, so it is context, not a counterexample.

reviews.rationale: The contract's reading is not fair to the speaker. Under a fair reading, which requires a general-purpose alternative paradigm, the claim has no defined capability threshold, and the narrow robot-learning evidence neither contradicts nor supports it. So it cannot be scored as drafted.
